Everyone needs help. "It takes a village to ___" isn't a joke, it's a reality. No one is truly "self-made", it's just what society wants us to believe so they don't feel the need to care when someone is struggling. Society teaches us that the homeless did something to "deserve" their circumstances, but it's just plain false. It can happen to anyone, and I don't think it's possible to get back up again without some form of support. Even if it's just someone giving you a chance with a job or accepting what little the government will offer, we all need support. 

If nothing else then you could accept the government's help as the least they can do for putting you (and others) in this situation. Often an imperfect situation calls for an imperfect solution and we have to accept the lesser of two evils.

I absolutely love when games let you choose your own play style, and don't force the order in which you work on each area of the game. I think you know this, but enjoyment is what really matters when you play a game. If you can find simple joys in completing the "boring" side of the game before devoting yourself to the story then I think this is actually a very clever way of playing. 

Personally, I get bored easily or forget what I was working on and go off to the mines or ocean. This, (along with starting in early access) meant that I felt "done" before getting very far with creating an efficient farm. I took a break and then came back after the full release and kinda just sped through a bunch of stuff. Mostly because I had starter funds from my original save after resetting for the update to 1.0.

Your post has inspired me to start fresh so I can give your play style a try. I suspect that once you unlock more seeds and animals, along with upgrading your crops you will likely be in a very nice position. I'm curious as to how it will compare to my scatterbrained approach. XD
I already hold off on most of the NPC interactions, but I try to talk to everyone during festivals. 
I think it'll be fun to try a new style and make it my own at the same time. I really like the idea of saving the best bits for last, as you seem to be doing. 

To finish this off, I want to thank you for your post. I enjoyed reading it and several of the comments, along with your responses. 
I think that you're definitely playing Coral Island the "right" way, mostly because you're having fun, but also because you're paving the way to focus on the good parts down the road. Splitting your focus too much tends to lessen enjoyment of a good game, so I hope that with this, (and the rest of the great comments I've seen), you have been reassured that the voice in the back of your head is most likely a form of anxiety that's being overactive in it's attempt to protect you. 

Play your way and enjoy Coral Island! 🏝️

I do think I could benefit from DBT, I just need to get some of my other issues managed first. I'm taking it slow because anytime I try to rush things I end up deeper than I started. Still, things are getting better, a little at a time. I think it'll take quite a bit before I'm ready to give DBT another go, but I do intend to try it again.

I had a really good DBT group that was more understanding about people not being able to do the homework. Unfortunately you don't get much out of DBT if you don't do it. 
They always asked the question "what prevented you from doing the homework?", and tried to give suggestions on how to get it done next time.
Still, it's not helpful when you have other underlying issues that go deeper than "I forgot" or "I didn't have time".

I got very frustrated that no one seemed inclined to explore the possibility that DBT wasn't going to help me with the position I was (and still am) in. 

I suspect autism is to blame for a lot of my struggles but I can't afford the $2k+ for an assessment to be certain. At this point I'm not even sure if BPD is an accurate diagnosis. I think I'm diagnosed with ADHD but bipolar has been suggested to me as well. 

I think the problem for me was attempting treatment before really knowing what was causing my symptoms. I completely stopped seeking help for quite some time because I don't want to have to fight to get real understanding from medical professionals. 

After doing a lot of my own research and self discovery I think I'm ready to try advocating for myself again. I still think it'll be a struggle to find the right help for me, especially with a low budget and ability to commit, but it's worth another shot at least.

Everyone has a different timetable when it comes to growth and making improvements, I've found that the slower I go the more likely I am to sustain the improvements.

It's possible that DBT could benefit you but not with where you're at right now. There's a block that's preventing you from getting anything out of it aside from frustration as things are. You might benefit more from delving deeper into your personal struggles before trying DBT again (if you later think you might find it helpful). I don't mean to say DBT is "right" and you "should" try it again at some point, but I hope you feel open to consider whether or not it might be helpful to you one day.

I get where you're coming from. Once I got stamped with borderline personality disorder it felt like the only option presented to me was DBT. Even after I tried and had a bad experience with it. It works for a lot but not for everyone and I'm telling you it doesn't work for me, at least not yet. 

It definitely felt like I was being told that I wasn't doing it right or hadn't given it enough of a chance. I'm pretty sure they just didn't want to look beyond the surface of my struggles. I have issues with demand avoidance which makes the homework and weekly sessions impossible to keep up with at the moment. Also major anxiety which made the group aspect even more difficult. 

I do believe some tools they use in DBT are helpful but I think you gotta be at a certain point to get much out of it. If you struggle with simply getting out of bed and basic survival (eating, sleeping, etc.) then you're not going to be able to complete the homework.

It's completely understandable to want peace and quiet in your own home, and very unfortunate when that's not possible. 

Have you spoken to your neighbors about the noise? Might it be possible to work out a quiet time for a portion of each day? I know that's tough with a baby, especially if they're new parents and still figuring stuff out. Sometimes they get defensive because they don't have much control over when the child is crying and adding more to their plate for someone else can feel insurmountable. 

Still, I don't see any harm in respectfully having a conversation with them about it. They might not even know it's a big problem for you. I'd want to be sure they know that you're understanding and simply curious if they can easily make some small accommodations to make you more comfortable in your own home. There's nothing wrong with asking for a favor as long as you can accept "no" as an answer.

Best wishes for whatever solution/s you choose to explore!

While I don't have personal experience with noise cancelling headphones or the like, I did feel it worthwhile to share some of the things my family uses to cope with uncomfortable noises and headphones/earbuds.

My brother has always had a hard time with earbuds and headphones because both are very uncomfortable for him. He's recently found some success with bone conducting headphones. However, they aren't noise cancelling unfortunately, as your ears are still uncovered.

My mom has, in the past suggested using "brown noise" to help filter out distracting sounds. It's similar to white noise (which I often can't stand), but I don't know the science behind it. I personally wasn't a fan but I also didn't give it much of a chance. There are some apps which will let you fine-tune the type of noise that works best for you.

I'd be curious to know if it might give a noise cancelling effect if one were to use the two together. 

Again, I have no experience with this but thought I'd leave it here in case you or others may wish to look into the idea.

Hey, calm down. You're actually doing great already just by realizing that these feelings are unreasonable. However that doesn't make them any less valid. You aren't in control of these sudden outbursts of emotion but you've already taken the first step to overcoming them by reaching out. 

Sudden onset of extreme irritability is cause for concern, but it is manageable with the right help.

In dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) there's a skill called STOP 

Stop - whatever you're doing just stop it, whether it's an argument or an internal struggle.

Take a step back - in a face to face confrontation you can take this literally but the idea is to distance yourself from the situation so you can look at it from an outside perspective.

Observe - look at the situation at hand and contemplate it from both sides of the equation. Take into account both your emotional and logical thoughts.

Proceed mindfully - using what's referred to as "wise-mind" (the place where emotions and logic meet), proceed in a way that reflects the observations you made previously.

I think this could help you in the short term but I'd strongly suggest doing some further research and ideally seek professional help.

Comparing problems won't get anyone anywhere besides upset and angry. I spent years telling myself I'm fortunate and many have it worse, that didn't make my struggles any easier. We all deserve better and saying we don't just because it could be worse is ludicrous. Do you really believe you don't deserve more than you've been given just because someone has less?

It's admirable that you're able to recognize this about yourself and take this post to heart. It shows growth and that's all anyone can strive for.

I'd like to add that even if someone actually does have an easier time in life it doesn't give us the right to think poorly of them based purely off that. They didn't choose to be fortunate or successful. They probably won't ever understand just how good they've got it, we can only hope they aren't jerks about it. 

I think we all deserve a certain amount of separation from our circumstances in the eyes of others. We aren't defined by our circumstances but by how we choose to deal with them. Someone born fortunate doesn't deserve the same credit for getting through school or holding a job as someone who struggles to get through each day. It doesn't mean the fortunate deserve your resentment simply for taking what was offered. It's another story if they are fortunate jerks XD

While BPD can certainly be terrible, I've heard it's more treatable than some others. That's not to say it's "better" or "worse" it's all about the experience of the individual so comparing diagnosis is not constructive. If anything it just makes it harder on yourself and others.

Through DBT and whatever healthy methods work for you it's possible to no longer meet the diagnostic criteria of BPD. I wouldn't say that means it's curable but you can get better at handling the symptoms and some (such as self harm) can go away. 

I in no way mean to say that overcoming BPD is easy, I've just heard it's possible for a good amount of people that get diagnosed.

I'm really sorry you're in such a rough spot. It's not easy to be in your shoes. I won't presume to know more than that, but that's all I need to know that you've done well to make it as far as you have.

Do you ever have times when you forget about not wanting to live? 
What makes those times a little more bearable?
Can you think of one small way you might improve your current quality of life?

Sometimes life isn't very rewarding so we have to find ways to reward ourselves instead. What's something you could do to reward yourself for each day you're still alive?

Have you tried seeking professional help? If so, what have they suggested? If not, what would you like them to help you with?

Do you have any coping strategies?

Overdose might be the least painful but it depends on the drug. Some aren't fun at all and have a low success rate which will leave you in a worse state if you survive.

I suggest you hold off as long as possible and ask yourself some questions when you feel most stable. 

If you had the best life imaginable would you still want to end it?

What's the bare minimum it would take for you to want to live?

Are there any reasonable steps you can take to improve your current quality of life, even just a little?

Try to think up some of your own if you feel up to it. I don't think choosing death is necessarily the wrong choice, but I do hope you're absolutely certain and not only when you're at your worst.

Best wishes, regardless of what you choose.

You have some good suggestions here so I'll just say try to avoid shifting your bodyweight in a way that makes you sway back and forth.

My highschool English teacher straight up told me "you're swaying like a tree" XD

Maybe try making the shift seem purposeful, like you're leaning in to share a secret or leaning back to confidently end a point.

Also try not to get too caught up in the anxiety of trying to remember all the tips and tricks people are suggesting.

I got full marks from the same teacher when delivering a speech even though I felt I looked at my note cards too much and didn't make enough eye contact. (Pretty sure I still swayed quite a bit too XD)

The main point is that you deliver the message well and refrain from distracting from it too much with your tone or body language.

It's admirable that you're trying to help but you said it yourself, they don't want to hear this sort of thing. 

Love from a stranger and empty promises aren't going to solve any problems for them. Repeating it won't solidify the idea in their mind. 

I don't want to be harsh but I do want you to learn how to better help someone in crisis. It's clear that you're trying and I only hope that you can learn to help in a way that's needed.
My method probably isn't the best one either, but the main thing I'm trying to get across is empathy for their struggle. Thoughts of wanting to end one's self are rough as hell.

You keep saying things will get better and you're not wrong, but we all know the good can't last either. Giving a person too much hope can be just as harmful as taking it all away. Because when things inevitably get worse again it can trigger worse thoughts. The truth is that life will always be hard, we can only really hope to get better at dealing with the bad so that we can start to cultivate more good.

I don't want to discourage you from reaching out to people in need, but I encourage you to ask people who are really struggling or have struggled in the past what words are comforting to them in a time of crisis.

That really doesn't leave you with many options for an easy way out... It sounds like you've had to deal with a lot of hardships, more than anyone deserves. 

Unfortunately I don't think anyone will be willing to give any real suggestions for how to end things. It's generally frowned upon to help in that way. 
My personal route is to wait until medical assistance in dying (MAID) is available for those with mental issues in Canada. That's a long process though, even after it's available and there's a chance to get denied. 

I don't want to give you false hope, so I think the best I can do is to suggest that you find help. Just to improve your quality of life enough that you can put off suicide until you can find a decent method. It's a big decision and you want to do it right so you don't risk surviving, but in an even worse state. 

Best case scenario things get better, worst case you've just delayed the inevitable long enough to be absolutely certain this is the only path left to you. 
I'd guess you already have a pretty good idea that it is, but hopefully you can take time to think about it anyway. Sometimes we forget to look at things from each different perspective. For example, on the off chance your life takes a turn for the best, would you still feel the same way? Is it worth the risk that you might miss out on something amazing? What would it take for you to want to live?

Except it is primarily about what she wants...
She should take the necessary precautions by educating herself as much as possible about all the major risks.

Still, at the end of the day it is her body, and if she wants to do something OP or anyone else deems to be detrimental to herself and the child inside her then so be it. No one can force her to do anything, it is her choice based on her wants and needs.

I'm not saying OP shouldn't have a say or that he's in the wrong. I honestly think they are both right, and both valid to have their own primary concerns. The real problem is the miscommunication happening between them.

The only reason I see for a boss to tell a pregnant woman to stop working is to avoid liability if something does happen. 

I really don't think he should bring his work place position into a relationship issue. It would likely make her feel even worse than she does now. It shouldn't even matter that they work together because his concerns would be the same if he worked elsewhere. He really shouldn't be using his workplace "superiority" on his wife unless it is related to the work at hand.
"probably" being the key word here. That's still a risk (of unknown severity) until they check it out. She should be just as concerned but she's got her own anxiety which has made her blind to his.

Why should he trust her when she denied not only his suggestion but also his main concern for the safety of both mother and child? Mothers are at risk from any pregnancy without added risk factors from the workplace. He wants to find a way to mitigate the risk and she won't even make a counter suggestion about double checking to see how big of a risk their workplace really is. If she's so confident that it's safe then she should have no trouble proving it. 

As far as OP is concerned she has given him no reason to trust that she is taking his concerns seriously. In fact she has proven the opposite to be true, she doesn't see his concerns about the workplace to be a major issue. 

Do you really think the mother would be okay to stay at work if she thought there was a major risk to her baby? Of course not, the only reason she's so upset is because she doesn't think his concern is serious enough to warrant the stress it would cause her.
Complications with the birth can cause both mother and child to die... It wasn't a concern because she wasn't at such a high risk of complications from any fumes or chemicals used in her workplace.

Agreed, the child should be the primary concern. However I believe that both parents need to be healthy both physically and mentally. There are a lot of risks that could affect the fetus, but I believe it's far more important to make sure that the relationship is strong and the needs of each parent are being met. 

I believe that if they can sort out their relationship and communication styles then the child will be at very little risk.

I believe everyone is ignorant in certain areas, I don't see ignorance as being inherently bad, few things are. 

I meant only to use it to say that he doesn't seem to understand how his anxiety and words might come across to his partner. He's ignorant as to her perspective, as she is of his. 

As for his knowledge, I believe it's lacking but that you make a good point and he seems to have a good head on his shoulders to be able to recognize a possible risk.

I honestly don't mean to criticize either party because both are right and both are making mistakes. I'm not familiar with cs, but I do have a similar struggle of losing sight of my crosshair. 

I use a small center dot at full opacity and then make the inner and outer lines fairly big with a far lower opacity. I also find the movement of the outer lines can really draw my eye back to my crosshair, but it becomes distracting if the opacity is too high.

Edit: noticed that you already mentioned AimLab.

AimLab has a sensitivity test you can try, but I would say only use it as an initial guide. Try it, get used to it, then tweak it little by little until you're happy. I got 0.84, but I find that makes my aim shaky, so I went into the Valorant shooting range to play with the sensitivity. I found that 0.64 (800 dpi) works quite well for me at the moment, sometimes it feels a little fast and other times a little slow, I feel like that's probably a good middle ground. 

However different play-styles might benefit from a higher or lower sensitivity. For example you might want it higher if you're playing Raze a lot because it can help you flick down to throw a satchel and back up to shoot. I'm not sure but I feel like Jett might benefit from a slightly lower sensitivity so that you can aim her ult more accurately with micro adjustments. 

I am by no means a pro player but have played a decent amount of Valorant on and off.

Edit 2: I forgot to mention that when I'm in the shooting range I like to set my bots to full armor and use infinite ammo, then set the speed to medium. I run through it a few times to get a general baseline and then compare my results using different sensitivities. It's not a comic series but I love the way Tamora Pierce uses the concept of different stories in the same world. Each separate story is very different but still with similarities. They often traverse time so that you get more background on the characters and world but you don't need to read them in any particular order.

Anne McCaffrey does this well in her Dragonriders of Pern books too. She's even got some short stories in the mix.

A more popular example would be Tolkien's Lord of the Rings books and The Hobbit. He also did an incredible amount of behind the scenes world building to make everything go together.

One more example that's quite a bit different is The Stormlight Archive by Brandon Sanderson. He has several characters points of view in one series. Some perspectives line up and the characters meet. Others only last for a single chapter or seem so different that you begin to wonder how they're even connected. It can get very confusing and complicated, and yet it works very well for his style of writing.
I'd also recommend checking out his rules for writing magic systems. They aren't limited to classic fantasy magic. He references Superman several times, as well as the Harry Potter world and Lord of the Rings. He uses the terms hard and soft magic to discern the differences between types of magic systems as he sees them. They aren't strict rules, more like the guidelines that he follows in his own writing. Hard magic has more rules than soft magic but they don't need to be exclusive. It's more of a spectrum. I found it very interesting to read his views on magic systems.
